EGY_1970_ndp_the_national_democratic_par: With the Open Door under way, Sadat needs a political vehicle to replace the Arab Socialist Union and its Nasserist baggage. The National Democratic Party gathers technocrats, provincial notables and loyal officials under one roof, promising continuity with stability. Critics note that the line between party and state grows ever thinner, and that patronage follows the party card.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_party_of_the_president: The new party belongs, in every meaningful sense, to the man at its head. Ministers, governors and mayors are drawn to the presidential banner, and the press learns to speak of the party as the natural voice of the nation. Whoever wishes to be heard in Cairo must first be heard within its ranks.
EGY_1970_ndp_pluralism_or_emergency: Sadat's state of institutions stands at a crossroads. One path allows opposition parties to exist, so long as they know their place; the other keeps the nation under emergency rule in the name of order. The choice will define what kind of republic Egypt becomes once the Nasserist single party is truly gone.
EGY_1970_ndp_controlled_pluralism: Opposition platforms, or minbars, are permitted to speak, to publish and to contest elections, though the dominant party keeps a firm hand on the rules of the game. Cairo wins applause from Western capitals for its opening, while the regime's loyalists grumble that licence has been granted to those who would undo the revolution.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_emergency_state: The emergency laws are kept in force, justified by terrorism, sectarian strife and the long confrontation with Israel. Police stations multiply and the Mukhabarat grows more confident in its reach. Order is bought at the price of liberties, and few in the ministries believe the exception will ever end.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_shura_council: A consultative upper chamber is created to lend the regime a deliberative face. Its members are appointed or elected in carefully managed contests, and include respected jurists, editors and elder statesmen. The Shura Council advises and polishes legislation, and gives the republic an air of institutional depth that critics doubt it truly possesses.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_opposition_press: Newspapers affiliated with the licensed opposition are allowed to sharpen their pens, lampooning ministers and probing the excesses of the Infitah. Editors test the limits of the permissible, and the censors test them in turn. The regime hopes that a safety valve will keep anger from boiling over into the streets.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_law_of_shame: A sweeping measure against behaviour deemed damaging to the nation's values lets the state prosecute critics for disgracing the country at home or abroad. Under the banner of protecting public morals, writers, preachers and politicians alike discover that dissent may now be treated as a matter of honour, and punished accordingly.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_september_arrests: In a single sweep, the security services detain Islamists, leftists, Copts, journalists and old politicians by the hundreds. The president declares that he is defending the state against sectarian strife and subversion, but the cells fill with men of every persuasion, and the grudges they carry will outlast the regime that jailed them.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_islamist_bargain: The regime seeks peace with the religious current it once feared. Preachers are given airtime, al-Azhar is courted, and the Brotherhood is tolerated in return for its restraint. Many in the establishment see a pragmatic accommodation; others warn that Cairo is feeding the very movement that may one day turn on it.
EGY_1970_ndp_crush_the_gamaat: The militant groups of Upper Egypt and the Cairo slums are declared enemies of the state. Security units sweep through the villages of the south, while informers and interrogators work in the cellars of the capital. The government promises that the gunmen will be rooted out, whatever the cost to the rule of law.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_succession_question: No president rules forever, and in Cairo the question of what follows is whispered in every salon and barracks. The party, the army and the civil bureaucracy each hold a claim to the legacy. The decision, once taken, will shape the republic for a generation.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_vice_presidents_hour: The former air force commander, loyal and cautious, steps from the shadow of the presidency into its centre. Hosni Mubarak promises continuity without adventure, and the officer corps, relieved to see one of its own in the palace, closes ranks behind him. The nation breathes out, and waits to see what manner of ruler he will prove.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_party_machine: The apparatus that Sadat built chooses its own man. Fouad Mohieddin, secretary-general of the party and a master of committees and compromise, takes the presidency as the candidate of the organisation rather than the barracks. Governors and local bosses welcome him, though the generals watch with narrowed eyes.
EGY_1970_ndp_a_civilian_successor: In a break with the long tradition of officers in the palace, the presidency passes to a civilian. Mustafa Khalil, the experienced prime minister and a favourite of Western governments, promises clean administration and sober diplomacy. The army grumbles at the slight, but foreign capitals are quick to offer their approval.
EGY_1970_ndp_presidential_term_limits: The constitution is amended so that the head of state may stand for office again and again. Loyalists describe it as a safeguard against instability in dangerous times, while opponents see only a monarchy in republican dress. The new article is passed with little real debate.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_state_of_institutions: Egypt is at last presented as a state of institutions, with a dominant party, a managed parliament, an open economy and a settled place in the world. Whether it is a modern republic or merely an elegant façade remains a matter for the historians, but for now the machinery of government runs smoothly.
EGY_1970_ndp_law_43_expanded: Law 43 of 1974 opened the door to foreign capital, and now the government widens it further. Tax holidays, guarantees against nationalisation and simpler licensing are offered to investors from the Gulf and the West. Cairo is betting that private money will do what the socialist state never managed.
EGY_1970_ndp_joint_ventures_with_the_wes: Western firms are invited to partner with Egyptian companies in factories and assembly plants along the Nile. German engineers, French manufacturers and American suppliers arrive with capital and technical expertise. The old public sector looks on warily as a new class of managers and middlemen rises beside it.
EGY_1970_ndp_open_the_banking_sector: Foreign and joint-venture banks are licensed to operate in Cairo and Alexandria, financing trade, construction and imports. The bankers bring credit and new methods, along with a new set of interests at the president's table. Nasser's closed financial system is quietly left behind.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_new_cities: Out in the desert, far from the crowded Nile Valley, new towns rise from the sand: the Tenth of Ramadan, Sadat City, the Sixth of October. Planners promise factories, housing and a release for the overcrowded capital. Sceptics point to the cost, and wonder whether anyone will wish to live so far from Cairo.
EGY_1970_ndp_export_processing_zones: Special zones are set aside near Suez and Alexandria, where companies can import and export with minimal customs and bureaucratic delay. Investors are drawn by the lighter regulation and the cheap labour of the Delta. For the government, they are a showcase of what a modern, outward-looking Egypt can offer.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_gulf_of_suez_oil_boom: With the Sinai wells and the Gulf of Suez fields back in Egyptian hands, foreign drilling consortia arrive in force. Rigs crowd the waters off the coast, and crude begins to flow in earnest. Oil becomes the lifeblood of a state long starved of foreign exchange, though it also breeds a dangerous reliance on a single commodity.
EGY_1970_ndp_an_open_economy: The Infitah has matured into a settled strategy. Imports fill the shop windows, foreign banks and hotels dominate the skyline, and a new bourgeoisie flourishes in the cities. The government declares that Egypt has rejoined the world economy, even as the fellahin ask what has changed in their villages.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_food_security_programme: A country that cannot feed its own people cannot be master of its own destiny. Cairo turns to American grain under Public Law 480, hoping that wheat shipments and new agricultural measures will keep bread on the table. The price is a deeper dependence on the goodwill of Washington.
EGY_1970_ndp_subsidy_reform: The subsidies on bread, oil and sugar, a pillar of the Nasserist social bargain, are becoming unaffordable. International lenders demand cuts and the treasury agrees. But the poor of Cairo remember the riots of 1977, and every price rise is watched anxiously from the palace windows.
EGY_1970_ndp_privatise_tourism: The pyramids, the temples of Luxor and the beaches of the Red Sea are Egypt's most reliable assets. The state hands hotels and tourist enterprises to private operators, in the hope that profit will bring investment and visitors. Foreign currency flows in, though the benefits reach some Egyptians more than others.
EGY_1970_ndp_expand_the_universities: New campuses rise in the provinces and thousands more students pass through lecture halls built for hundreds. The government promises that a degree will still guarantee a post, though the graduates already outnumber the jobs on offer. Education remains the great promise of the republic, and its greatest source of disappointment.
EGY_1970_ndp_jehans_law: Jehan Sadat, the president's wife, champions reforms to the personal status laws, giving women greater rights in divorce, custody and the home. Liberals applaud and reformers take heart, but the ulema are scandalised, and critics mock the measures as Jehan's law, imposed by decree on a society not yet persuaded.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_jerusalem_initiative: In a gesture that stuns the world, the president announces that he is ready to travel to Jerusalem itself and speak before the Knesset. It is a gamble of extraordinary daring, aimed at regaining the Sinai and ending the cycle of war. The Arab world is appalled, but in Egypt, many weary families dare to hope.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_camp_david_dividend: Peace brings rewards in its train. Washington opens its arsenals and its treasury to Egypt, and American aid flows toward the army and the economy alike. The president insists that the nation has been repaid for its courage, even as the Arab capitals denounce the bargain.
EGY_1970_ndp_bright_star: American and Egyptian troops train side by side in the desert, in exercises that would have been unthinkable a few years before. Egyptian officers learn Western doctrine, and the hardware of the Soviet era is gradually set aside. The army becomes a partner of the United States in everything but name.
EGY_1970_ndp_americas_shield: Egypt takes its place as the cornerstone of American strategy in the region. Military advisers, aircraft and credit follow, and Cairo is expected to support American interests in return. The alliance provides security and prosperity, though many Egyptians ask who now holds the real power on the Nile.
EGY_1970_ndp_return_to_the_arab_fold: Years after the break over the peace with Israel, Cairo works to mend its ties with the Arab capitals. Envoys travel to Riyadh, Amman and Baghdad, and the old quarrels are softened by Egypt's size and weight. The Arab League returns to the Nile, and Egypt resumes its place at the centre of the Arab world.
EGY_1970_ndp_mediterranean_friends: Egypt looks northward across the sea, cultivating friendships in Paris, Rome and Athens. Trade delegations, cultural exchanges and quiet diplomacy build a web of goodwill on the Mediterranean shore. For a regime keen to balance its American ties, these ancient neighbours offer welcome partnership.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_central_security_forces: A large force of conscript policemen is raised to guard government buildings, quell demonstrations and watch the streets. They are drawn from the poorest villages and housed in cramped barracks. The state gains a loyal truncheon, but this instrument of order depends on men who have little reason to love it.
EGY_1970_ndp_pay_the_conscripts: Recognising that the men of the security forces are the foundation of the regime's security, the ministry raises their wages and improves their housing. The conscripts remain loyal, and the interior ministry gains a reputation for looking after its own. The treasury grumbles, but the streets stay calm.
EGY_1970_ndp_cheap_order: The security conscripts are kept on a meagre wage and a poor diet, and the ministry puts its trust in discipline over generosity. The savings are welcome, but resentment festers in the barracks. Officers warn that men who are hungry and humiliated may one day turn their weapons on those who command them.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_suez_canal_expansion: The canal, silent and blocked for years, is reopened and widened for the largest ships of a new age. Dredgers work day and night, and engineers plan for a waterway that will carry the commerce of three continents. Egypt's gateway between East and West becomes once more the pride of the nation and its richest asset.
EGY_1970_ndp_the_cairo_international_fai: The fairgrounds of Nasr City fill with exhibitors from across the Mediterranean, the Gulf and beyond. Merchants haggle over textiles, machinery and cotton, while diplomats and ministers hold quiet talks over coffee. For the government, the fair is a shop window displaying an Egypt open for business.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_new_wafd: The old party of Saad Zaghlul, banned since the revolution of 1952, returns to the political stage. Fouad Serageddin, the aged Pasha who once served the monarchy, rallies the liberals, landowners and professionals who never forgot the parliamentary years. The New Wafd promises constitutional rule, free enterprise and respect for the law.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_wafdist_cabinet: With Serageddin at the helm, the Wafd forms a government drawn from the lawyers, merchants and veteran politicians of the liberal age. The ministries fill with men who remember the days of the constitution of 1923. The country watches to see whether the old guard can govern a modern republic.
EGY_1970_wafd_old_guard_or_young_wafd: The party faces a question about itself. Should it rely on the experienced pashas and landed families who kept the faith through the long years of exile, or give way to a new generation of lawyers and engineers eager to modernise? The answer will determine what the Wafd is to be.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_old_guard: The veterans of the pre-revolutionary parliament take charge of the party's direction, bringing with them dignity, land and long memories. Landowners flock to the banner, expecting that the estates seized by Nasser's reforms will receive a kinder hearing. The party gains steadiness, and a reputation for looking backwards.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_young_wafd: Younger lawyers, economists and engineers push the old men aside, bringing new ideas and fresh faces to the Wafd. They speak of a modern, European-minded Egypt with a free market and a free press. The pashas mutter about the loss of tradition, but the party gains the energy of a movement that expects to win.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_spirit_of_1923: The liberal constitution of 1923 is invoked as the foundation of the new order. Free elections, rights for all citizens and a government answerable to parliament are restored as the nation's guiding principles. The Wafd declares that the revolution has at last come home.
EGY_1970_wafd_an_independent_judiciary: The courts are freed from the control of the executive and the judges are assured of their tenure. Corrupt officials discover that the law now reaches them, and investors, foreign and domestic, begin to trust that contracts will be honoured. Egypt's proud legal tradition is restored to its place of honour.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_free_press_act: Censorship is lifted and the press is free to praise or condemn the government as it sees fit. Newspapers of every colour spring up in Cairo, and the coffee houses buzz with argument. Ministers learn the discomfort of being criticised in public, and the nation learns the habit of debate.
EGY_1970_wafd_parliamentary_government: Power rests firmly with the elected assembly and the ministers who answer to it. The president is a dignified figure above the fray, and the cabinet rises and falls by the will of the deputies. The Wafd has realised the oldest dream of Egyptian liberalism, though a restive nation must learn how to live with it.
EGY_1970_wafd_crescent_and_cross: The Wafd was born in 1919 under the banner of the crescent embracing the cross, uniting Muslim and Copt in the cause of independence. Its heirs revive that vision of a national community open to all. The Coptic minority, long uneasy under the revolution, welcomes the pledge of equal citizenship.
EGY_1970_wafd_secular_courts: The Wafd moves to place civil law above religious jurisdiction, with a single system of national courts for all Egyptians. Lawyers hail a modern reform, but the scholars of al-Azhar protest that the faith is being pushed from public life. The government answers that justice must be the same for all.
EGY_1970_wafd_end_the_sequestrations: The property seized by the revolution, from estates to town houses and factories, is returned to those who lost it. Merchants and shopkeepers rejoice, and a confident middle class emerges. The landless fellahin, who benefited from the old land reforms, look on with unease at the return of the old owners.
EGY_1970_wafd_bank_misr_reborn: Talaat Harb founded Bank Misr to build an Egyptian capitalism free of foreign dominance. The Wafd revives his dream, encouraging the bank and its industries to grow once more. Factories rise in Alexandria and the Delta, and the old ideal of a prosperous national economy gains fresh life.
EGY_1970_wafd_egyptianise_industry: Egyptian owners and managers are encouraged to take the lead in the nation's industry, with preference given to national firms over foreign ones. Taxes are eased on domestic enterprise, and a class of native industrialists comes into its own. The Wafd insists that a free economy and a national economy need not be opposed.
EGY_1970_wafd_reopen_the_cotton_exchange: In Alexandria, the cotton exchange, shuttered during the years of state control, opens its doors once more. Brokers and growers gather in the old trading halls to bargain over the white gold of the Nile. The market returns, and with it the prosperity and cosmopolitan air of the old Mediterranean port.
EGY_1970_wafd_alexandria_free_port: Alexandria, once the most cosmopolitan city in the Mediterranean, is declared a free port. Ships unload without heavy duty, merchants of every nation set up offices, and warehouses fill along the harbour. The city of the Greeks, Italians and Levantines stirs again, and dreams of its former splendour.
EGY_1970_wafd_modern_agriculture_societi: Cooperative societies, backed by credit and technical advice, help the fellahin to modernise their farming. New seeds, machinery and marketing arrangements ease the burden on smallholders. The Wafd hopes to prove that a free economy can serve the peasant as well as the pasha.
EGY_1970_wafd_a_liberal_economy: Prices, trade and enterprise are freed from the grip of the state, and the economy responds with vigour. Egyptian goods find buyers abroad, investment pours in, and the bazaars thrive. The Wafd points to prosperity as proof that liberalism and national dignity go hand in hand.
EGY_1970_wafd_friends_in_london_and_pari: The Wafd has always looked toward Europe, and its leaders still count friends in Whitehall and the Quai d'Orsay. Old acquaintances are renewed, loans are discussed, and the memories of the bitter quarrel over Suez are set quietly aside. Egypt takes its place among the liberal powers of the Mediterranean.
EGY_1970_wafd_sudan_brotherhood: The unity of the Nile Valley was a Wafdist ideal long before the revolution, and the party now reaches out to Khartoum in a spirit of friendship. Trade, water and political partnership are on the table. The Sudanese, long wary of Egyptian domination, are cautiously receptive to a more respectful tone.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_liberal_age_returns: The parliament sits, the courts rule, the press argues and the markets trade. A generation after the revolution closed it, Egypt's liberal age has returned in a new guise. The task now is to prove that the freedoms of the past can survive the pressures of the present.
EGY_1970_wafd_a_national_army: The army is placed under civilian authority and trained as a professional national force, free from the intrigues of the officer corps. Barracks politics are discouraged and merit is rewarded. The generals accept the new order with reserve, aware that the Wafd has ended the age of the soldier-president.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_wafd_succession: Serageddin is old, and the party knows that the time must come when a new leader must take his place. The Wafd has little tradition of handing on power gracefully. The choice of successor will reveal whether the party is a movement of ideas or merely the following of one man.
EGY_1970_wafd_a_young_leader: The party turns to a younger man, a lawyer or economist untouched by the quarrels of the past. His speeches speak of the future rather than the glories of 1919, and the new generation of voters responds. The old pashas bow their heads, persuaded that the party has chosen to survive.
EGY_1970_wafd_the_pashas_heir: Leadership passes to a scion of the great landed families, a man whose name is known in every village of the Delta. He carries the prestige of the old Wafd and the loyalty of its notables. He is a guardian of the party's heritage, though reform may have to wait.
EGY_1970_lib_the_liberal_cabinet: Mustafa Kamel Murad and his Liberal Socialist allies take office with a bold promise to dismantle the heavy hand of the state and let the market breathe. The ministers speak of competition, enterprise and sound money. After years of socialism, Cairo's business community is cautiously delighted.
EGY_1970_lib_the_liberal_programme: The cabinet unveils its programme of free markets, lean government and individual choice. Business leaders applaud, Western economists nod approval, and the trade unions grow nervous. It is a bold vision of a very different Egypt, and the government must now decide how swiftly to pursue it.
EGY_1970_lib_shock_or_gradual: The reformers are divided on how fast to move. Some urge a sudden break with the controlled economy, cutting prices, subsidies and tariffs at a stroke; others favour a patient transition that spares the poor. The decision will shape the nation's economy and the government's fate.
EGY_1970_lib_market_shock: Prices are freed, subsidies are slashed and the state steps back at once. The economy convulses, shops empty and fill again at higher prices, and families on fixed incomes suffer. The government insists that the pain is the price of recovery, and asks the nation to endure.
EGY_1970_lib_gradual_liberalisation: Controls are lifted step by step, with warnings given and cushions provided for the vulnerable. Businesses adapt, workers adjust, and the government keeps a watchful eye on the street. Progress is slower than the zealots wish, but it is less likely to end in riots.
EGY_1970_lib_reopen_the_stock_exchange: The old exchanges of Cairo and Alexandria, among the oldest in the region, reopen their trading floors. Brokers return in dark suits, and shares in Egyptian companies change hands once more. A new generation of investors discovers that wealth can be made on paper as well as in the cotton fields.
EGY_1970_lib_privatise_public_firms: The great state enterprises of the Nasser years, from textile mills to steelworks, are offered for sale to private buyers. Efficiency improves and revenues flow into the treasury, but workers fear for their jobs and the unions threaten to strike. The government presses ahead, convinced that the state is a poor businessman.
EGY_1970_lib_light_regulations: Licences are simplified, red tape is cut and inspectors are told to give guidance rather than punishment. Businessmen find it easier to open a shop, hire workers and import goods. Critics fear for safety and fair dealing, but entrepreneurs praise a government that gets out of the way.
EGY_1970_lib_tax_cuts_for_growth: Taxes are lowered on households and firms alike, in the belief that money left in private hands will be put to better use than the state could manage. Shopkeepers, merchants and professionals feel the difference at once. The treasury trusts that growth will fill the gap.
EGY_1970_lib_unify_the_exchange_rate: The tangle of official and black-market exchange rates is swept away, and the pound is allowed to find its own level. Exporters and importers can plan with confidence, and foreign investors take note. The change is painful for those who lived off the old distortions.
EGY_1970_lib_agricultural_price_liberali: The state no longer fixes the price of cotton, wheat or rice. Farmers sell to the highest bidder and decide for themselves what to plant. Some fellahin prosper, while others fall into debt, and the villages discover the rewards and risks of the market.
EGY_1970_lib_open_egypt_to_the_world: Customs barriers fall, visas are eased and foreign companies are invited to open offices in Cairo and the Nile Valley. Skyscrapers of glass and steel rise beside the old city. The nation that once shut itself behind socialist walls now presents itself as a crossroads of commerce.
EGY_1970_lib_a_market_economy: The planners and the controllers of the old regime have been replaced by prices, profits and competition. The economy hums with a vitality that surprises even its architects. Egypt has become, in outlook if not entirely in practice, a market society.
EGY_1970_lib_civil_liberties_act: A charter of rights guarantees free speech, free assembly and the protection of the courts. Political prisoners are released, and opposition parties emerge from the shadows. The government declares that a free economy requires a free society, and invites the nation to judge its record.
EGY_1970_lib_decentralise_the_governorat: Power is devolved from the ministries of Cairo to the governorates, which receive greater authority over their budgets and local affairs. Provincial governors, long the creatures of the capital, now answer to local councils. Reformers hail the end of the centralised state, though some fear regional rivalry.
EGY_1970_lib_european_partnership: Egypt turns toward the nations of the European continent, seeking trade, investment and technology. Delegations are exchanged with Paris, Bonn and Rome, and the cabinet speaks of a Mediterranean future. The relationship is built on shared commercial interest and a common wish for stability.
EGY_1970_lib_the_eec_association: Negotiators travel to Brussels to discuss a formal association with the European Economic Community. The prospect of tariff-free access to the markets of the Six excites manufacturers and growers alike. Whether Europe will accept is a question of diplomacy, but the ambition itself marks a new direction for Egypt.
EGY_1970_lib_the_market_republic: The liberal government has remade the republic in its own image, with open markets, decentralised power and close ties to Europe. Egyptians are told that they now live in a modern, competitive nation. Prosperity is uneven, but the direction of travel seems unmistakable.
EGY_1970_lib_a_smaller_army: The cabinet argues that a nation at peace with the market has no need of an enormous standing army. The size of the forces is reduced and funds are directed to training and organisation. The officers resent the cuts, but the finance ministry notes with approval that the army now costs far less.
EGY_1970_lib_western_equipment: Out go the ageing Soviet tanks and aircraft, and in come modern weapons from the West. The army's technicians must learn new systems, and the purchases are costly. But the generals admit that Western equipment is the equal of any arrayed against them, and the government wins friends abroad.
EGY_1970_lib_the_liberal_succession: The liberal programme has been delivered, and the government must now decide how to carry it forward. Should the party seek partners to share the burden of power, or trust its own majority? The coming choice will determine whether liberalism in Egypt is a consensus or a creed.
EGY_1970_lib_a_grand_coalition: The liberals reach out to the New Wafd, and the two parties govern together in the name of constitutional rule and a free economy. The coalition brings stability and a broad base of support, though it also demands compromise on matters the liberals might prefer to settle themselves.
EGY_1970_lib_govern_alone: The liberals decline to share power, trusting in their own majority and their own vision. Decisions are made swiftly and the programme is carried forward without dilution. Critics warn that a government accountable to no partner may find itself accountable to no one.
EGY_1970_slp_the_labour_government: Ibrahim Shukri leads the Socialist Labour Party into government, with a promise to defend the workers and fellahin in an age of change. A former Nasserist minister turned reformer, he speaks of social justice, honest government and a fair share for the poor. The trade unions throw their weight behind him.
EGY_1970_slp_the_labour_programme: The new government sets out its programme of social reform, mixing the heritage of Egyptian socialism with a commitment to political freedom. Welfare, wages and public services are placed at the centre of policy. The party hopes to prove that a left-wing government can be both humane and efficient.
EGY_1970_slp_labour_or_islamic_socialism: The party faces a question of identity. Is it a secular movement of workers and trade unionists in the tradition of European labour parties, or a movement that grounds its socialism in the moral language of Islam? The answer will decide whom it can speak for.
EGY_1970_slp_labour_socialism: The party draws on the traditions of the European labour movement, stressing class solidarity, trade unions and the rights of working people. Factory delegates and union officials set the tone of debate. Egyptian socialism is recast as a democratic and secular cause, and Western social democrats take note.
EGY_1970_slp_islamic_socialism: The party presents social justice as a duty ordained by religion, and calls for an economy guided by the Islamic ideals of charity and fairness. The alliance with the Muslim Brotherhood, once unthinkable, brings votes and moral authority. Secular comrades protest that socialism has been handed to the preachers.
EGY_1970_slp_free_unions: The unions are freed from state control and allowed to choose their own leaders and conduct their own bargaining. Long-suppressed grievances find a voice in the factories of Helwan and Mahalla. Workers stand taller, while employers learn to negotiate with men who can no longer be ordered about.
EGY_1970_slp_the_social_dialogue_council: Employers, unions and ministers are brought together around one table to hammer out the terms of the nation's economic life. The council gives the workers a voice and the businessmen a hearing. Compromise, not command, becomes the style of policy, and industrial peace the reward.
EGY_1970_slp_a_social_contract: The government offers the people a pact: a decent wage, secure employment and basic services in exchange for loyalty and effort. It echoes the promises of the revolution, but without the coercion that came with them. The question is whether the state can afford to keep its word.
EGY_1970_slp_workers_rights_act: A new law guarantees workers a fair contract, a safe workplace and protection against dismissal. Factory owners complain of rigidity, but the men on the shop floor see a sign that their labour is respected. The statute book finally speaks the language of the labour movement.
EGY_1970_slp_progressive_income_tax: Those who earn more are asked to contribute more, in a tax system designed to share the burden according to ability. The wealthy of Zamalek and Maadi protest, while the treasury welcomes a reliable stream of revenue. The government calls it simple justice.
EGY_1970_slp_pension_reform: Elderly workers and widows are promised a secure income in their retirement, funded by contributions and general taxation. The system is extended to farm labourers and the self-employed, who were long left out. In a country where families have always cared for their own, the state now shares the burden.
EGY_1970_slp_healthcare_for_the_fellahin: Clinics and rural hospitals are built in the villages of the Delta and the Said, where the nearest doctor was once a day's journey away. Nurses and midwives are trained in the thousands. The government says the fellahin built the nation, and now the nation will care for them.
EGY_1970_slp_cooperative_banks: Village banks owned by the farmers themselves offer loans on fair terms, breaking the grip of moneylenders and merchants. Smallholders are able to buy seed and fertiliser without falling into debt. The cooperative movement, long a hope of the left, begins to deliver.
EGY_1970_slp_public_housing_programme: New apartment blocks rise on the edge of the capital, built by the state and let at modest rents. Families long crowded into tenements or the tombs of the Cairo cemeteries receive keys to homes of their own. The programme is costly, but the government considers it a promise of the revolution at last redeemed.
EGY_1970_slp_a_mixed_economy: Neither a command economy nor a free-for-all, the new order combines public enterprise, private initiative and cooperative effort. Strategic industries remain in the hands of the state, while the market is trusted to supply the rest. The government hopes to prove that a middle way can work.
EGY_1970_slp_the_socialist_international: Egypt's labour government is welcomed into the company of Europe's social democratic parties. Delegates exchange visits with their counterparts in Stockholm, Bonn and Vienna, bringing advice, sympathy and the hope of investment. The party finds friends who share its ideals, and a legitimacy that Moscow could never confer.
EGY_1970_slp_mediterranean_social_democr: Egypt reaches out to the socialist and social democratic governments of the northern Mediterranean, finding common cause in the defence of workers and the welfare state. Cairo, Paris, Madrid and Athens speak of a shared southern European model. The sea becomes a bridge between old labour movements.
EGY_1970_slp_social_democracy_on_the_nil: After long effort, Egypt has become a social democracy on the Nile, with free unions, a mixed economy and a welfare state. The model is neither Moscow's nor Washington's, but its own. The nation looks on with pride, and the Arab world watches with interest.
EGY_1970_slp_a_peoples_army: The armed forces are recast as an army of citizens, in which service is a duty of every man and promotion rests on merit. Officers are taught that their loyalty lies with the people and the constitution. The government hopes to build a force that defends the republic rather than rules it.
EGY_1970_slp_veterans_of_october: The men who crossed the canal and fought in Sinai are honoured with pensions, medals and a place in public life. The government pays tribute to their sacrifice, and the veterans in turn become a pillar of support. The memory of the fighting is cherished as the foundation of national pride.
EGY_1970_slp_the_labour_succession: The founding generation of labour leaders is ageing, and the party must settle the course it will follow. Should it remain the organ of the factory floor, or become a broader movement of all Egyptians who work for a living? The decision shapes its future.
EGY_1970_slp_a_workers_party: The party sharpens its focus on the industrial workers, strengthening its ties with the trade unions and the factory committees. The movement becomes disciplined and class-conscious, and the unions have a government that is truly theirs. The middle classes look on with suspicion.
EGY_1970_slp_a_peoples_party: The party opens its doors to clerks, teachers, farmers and shopkeepers, and presents itself as the voice of the whole people. Its message is broad and its appeal wide. The unions sometimes grumble that the workers are lost in the crowd, but the ballot boxes fill.
EGY_1970_azh_the_council_of_scholars: The revolution has taken a religious turn, and the highest authority in the land now sits in the great mosque. A council of scholars from al-Azhar, led by Grand Imam Abd al-Halim Mahmud, takes over the guidance of the state. The law of God is to be the law of Egypt, and the ulema its guardians.
EGY_1970_azh_the_grand_imam_as_head_of_s: The Grand Imam, long the foremost religious figure of the Sunni world, assumes the highest office of the state. Egyptians who once looked to the president for guidance now look to the pulpit. It is an experiment without precedent in the modern age, watched with awe and alarm abroad.
EGY_1970_azh_azhar_or_riyadh: Two models of religious rule beckon. One is the learned, moderate tradition of al-Azhar, rooted in a thousand years of scholarship; the other is the austere pattern of the Arabian kingdom, rich in oil and in conviction. The path chosen will define the character of the Islamic state.
EGY_1970_azh_scholarly_rule: The scholars of the old university govern in the manner of their forebears, with deliberation, tradition and respect for the schools of law. They claim that Egypt's Islam is the Islam of moderation and learning. The state becomes a seminar, and ministers speak the language of the madrasa.
EGY_1970_azh_the_saudi_model: Envoys arrive from Riyadh with advice, funds and preachers of the Najdi school. The religious police patrol the markets, and the ulema are guided by teachings from the Arabian peninsula. Egypt's older, gentler traditions are thrust aside, and many scholars of al-Azhar mutter that the Nile has been made a tributary of the desert.
EGY_1970_azh_sharia_courts: The civil codes inherited from Napoleonic France are set aside, and the courts apply the law of the Sharia. Judges are learned in religion rather than statute, and punishments follow the classical rules. Supporters say the courts are now incorruptible; critics say they are medieval.
EGY_1970_azh_the_fatwa_council: A body of senior scholars is empowered to issue binding opinions on matters of law and public policy. Ministers consult them before they act, and their rulings are read from the pulpits. The state gains moral authority, and the scholars gain a power over government that no cleric has held in generations.
EGY_1970_azh_hisba_committees: Volunteers and officials patrol the streets, enforcing public morals in the name of commanding the good and forbidding the evil. Shopkeepers close for prayer, and cafes and cinemas are watched with suspicion. The pious applaud, while the secular and the cosmopolitan keep their heads down.
EGY_1970_azh_the_dhimma_question: The status of Egypt's Christian minority is raised anew. The traditional protections of the dhimma, with their taxes and restrictions, are debated in the councils of the faithful. The Copts, who have lived on the Nile since before Islam, view the discussion with fear and dismay.
EGY_1970_azh_the_zakat_treasury: The Islamic alms tax is collected by the state and distributed to the needy, the orphan and the traveller. Charity becomes a pillar of public finance, and the poor look to the mosque rather than the ministry. The government hopes that piety will succeed where bureaucracy has struggled.
EGY_1970_azh_waqf_restoration: The religious endowments seized by the revolution in the 1950s are returned to the care of the scholars. Lands, shops and buildings once again support mosques, schools and hospitals. The ulema regain an independent income, and a power they have not enjoyed in a generation.
EGY_1970_azh_islamic_banking_law: Interest is forbidden and the banks of Egypt must operate on the principles of profit-sharing and partnership. Financiers struggle to adapt, while devout depositors welcome institutions they can trust in conscience. The experiment is watched closely in the Gulf, and with some alarm in the West.
EGY_1970_azh_halal_trade_with_the_gulf: Merchants of Cairo and Alexandria find eager partners in the wealthy states of the Gulf, who share their faith and their preferences. Trade in food, textiles and goods certified in accordance with the law grows quickly. Egypt rediscovers its place in the commerce of the Muslim world.
EGY_1970_azh_the_pilgrim_economy: Every year, vast numbers of pilgrims pass through Egyptian ports and roads on their way to Mecca. The state improves the harbours and highways along the Red Sea and offers services to the faithful. What was once a trickle of devotion becomes a steady source of livelihood.
EGY_1970_azh_an_economy_of_faith: Zakat, waqf and halal trade together form a distinct economic order, built on faith and fairness rather than interest and speculation. The prosperity it brings is modest but widely shared. The ulema proclaim that the blessings of heaven have come to the Nile.
EGY_1970_azh_the_azhar_university_system: Al-Azhar's colleges multiply across the land, teaching religion and modern subjects side by side. Young men and women from the villages gain access to learning they never had. The old university becomes the foundation of a national school system.
EGY_1970_azh_a_religious_curriculum: Schools across the republic are directed to teach the Quran, the traditions of the Prophet and the Islamic sciences at the heart of the syllabus. The young are raised in the faith of their fathers. Scientists and engineers worry that modern studies are being squeezed aside.
EGY_1970_azh_the_riyadh_axis: Egypt's scholars seek a pact with the kingdom of Arabia, pledging to defend the faith and the holy places together. The two great centres of Sunni Islam, one of learning and one of wealth, join in common purpose. The prospect of oil money delights the treasury and unsettles Cairo's secular elite.
EGY_1970_azh_mission_to_africa: Preachers and teachers trained at al-Azhar travel south along the Nile and beyond, to Sudan, Chad, Ethiopia and Nigeria. They open schools, build mosques and spread the message of the scholars. Egypt's old role as the teacher of Africa's Muslims is revived.
EGY_1970_azh_the_state_of_al_azhar: The ancient university has become a state, and the state has become a university. Law, finance, education and morals are all governed by the doctrine of the scholars. Egypt stands as the world's greatest experiment in clerical rule, admired by some and feared by many more.
EGY_1970_ij_the_neglected_duty: The pamphlet of Muhammad Abd al-Salam Faraj declares that jihad is the forgotten pillar of the faith, and that the rulers of Egypt have forfeited their right to obedience. In its wake the state is overthrown and the men of the underground inherit the republic. The era of revolutionary Islam has begun.
EGY_1970_ij_the_emirs_shura: The leaders of the movement gather in secret councils to decide the fate of the nation. They consult one another in the manner of the early Muslim community, answerable to their consciences and their guns. Zeal binds the council together, though its members trust few outside it.
EGY_1970_ij_faraj_or_the_gamaa: The movement is divided. The conspirators of Cairo, led by Faraj, believe in the lightning strike from within the state, while the militants of Upper Egypt trust in popular mobilisation in the villages and universities. Only one vision can prevail.
EGY_1970_ij_farajs_vanguard: Faraj's disciplined cells take control of the state. Small, secret and fanatical, the vanguard sees itself as the only true believers in a sea of apostasy. It governs by conviction, suspicion and the sword, and soon the army and ministries are filled with uneasy faces.
EGY_1970_ij_the_gamaa_of_upper_egypt: The Gama'a Islamiyya, rooted in the villages of the Said and the student unions of Asyut and Minya, brings the revolution to the people. Its preachers and enforcers command a following among peasants and clerks alike. It governs through the mosque, the clan and the pulpit as much as through the ministries.
EGY_1970_ij_purge_the_army: Officers suspected of disloyalty or impiety are dismissed, arrested or worse. The barracks fill with whispers, and the cadets are taught the creed before they are taught the drill. The movement trusts only the soldiers it has remade in its own image.
EGY_1970_ij_abolish_the_parties: The parties that once crowded the political stage are declared un-Islamic divisions in the community of believers. Their offices are shuttered, their newspapers silenced and their leaders sent to prison or exile. A single movement, claiming to speak for God, now speaks for Egypt.
EGY_1970_ij_emirate_courts: Judges answerable to the emir apply a stern and swift justice, sweeping aside the delays and bribery of the old courts. Citizens who once despaired of the law find disputes settled in days. Theft is punished harshly and corruption is stamped out, though the price in mercy is high.
EGY_1970_ij_confiscate_the_infitah_fortu: The fortunes made during the Infitah by importers, contractors and middlemen are declared ill-gotten and seized by the new authority. The villas of the new rich are emptied and their bank accounts frozen. The poor cheer, while the merchant class flees or goes underground.
EGY_1970_ij_abolish_riba: Interest is outlawed in every transaction, and the banks are dissolved or reconstituted on Islamic principles. Foreign lenders withdraw in alarm, and the financial world looks on aghast. The emirate declares that it will live by the commandments of God, even if the money markets will not.
EGY_1970_ij_self_sufficiency: Egypt withdraws from the commerce of the infidel world and resolves to rely upon its own fields and workshops. Imports are curtailed, foreign goods are forbidden and ration cards are issued. The emirate calls this purity, and the shops, increasingly empty, call it hardship.
EGY_1970_ij_the_war_economy_of_the_emira: The whole economy is bent to the needs of the holy struggle. Factories turn out weapons and uniforms, farms deliver grain for the fighters and every household is called upon to sacrifice. The nation is on a permanent footing of war, and the emirate demands everything from its people.
EGY_1970_ij_export_the_revolution: Preachers, funds and weapons flow across the borders into Sudan, Libya, Syria and Jordan. The emirate holds that the revolution cannot stop at the Nile, and that every ruler of the region is a tyrant to be overthrown. Neighbouring capitals tremble, and the great powers take note.
EGY_1970_ij_break_with_riyadh: The emirate denounces the Saudi royal house as corrupt servants of the West and unworthy guardians of the holy places. Diplomats are expelled, the pilgrimage is disrupted and the oil wealth of Arabia is cut off. The breach is bitter, for Egypt's revolutionaries claim a leadership the kingdom will not yield.
EGY_1970_ij_war_on_the_occupier: Jerusalem and the lands of Palestine remain, in the eyes of the emirate, the first duty of every believer. Fighters are drawn from across the land, and preachers call for a holy war to liberate the holy places. For Israel, the neighbour on the Sinai frontier has become an implacable enemy.
EGY_1970_ij_the_emirate: The republic of Nasser and Sadat is gone, and in its place stands the Emirate of Egypt, ruled in the name of God by the men of the movement. Its achievements and its crimes alike are measured against a standard its founders set themselves. The world waits to see whether the emirate can endure.
EGY_1970_ij_the_mujahidin_army: Fighters hardened in the underground and the foreign wars of the faith are formed into an army of volunteers. They are inspired by faith and uninhibited by the habits of the old officer corps. Lacking organisation, the mujahidin make up for it in zeal.
EGY_1970_ij_weapons_of_the_jihad: Workshops in Cairo and the provinces turn out rifles, rockets and explosives for the holy struggle. Engineers loyal to the movement adapt the arsenal of the old army to new purposes. The emirate will not lack the tools of war, whatever the world may think.
EGY_1970_ij_the_emirs_succession: The movement's leaders must decide who will guide it in the years ahead. Two figures stand forth: the venerable blind preacher of the south, and the cold, ambitious physician who dreams of a worldwide struggle. The choice will decide whether the revolution stays on the Nile or sets out to conquer the world.
EGY_1970_ij_the_blind_sheikh: Omar Abd al-Rahman, the blind scholar of Upper Egypt, takes the helm. His sermons stir the multitudes in the mosques, and his authority is rooted in learning as much as in force. The emirate becomes a theocracy of the pulpit, in which the voice of the old sheikh is the voice of the state.
EGY_1970_ij_the_global_jihad: Ayman al-Zawahiri and his comrades turn the movement outward, building networks of cells and sympathisers from Sudan to Afghanistan and Yemen. Egypt becomes the base of a worldwide jihad against the West and its clients. The emirate no longer has frontiers, only fronts.
